questionsToConsider: Is this for a course, an incubator intake or a newsletter audience? Adjust the time and money questions to fit.
Which behaviours matter most in your programme, such as customer conversations, testing or commitment?
Do you want to follow up with people, and if so, should the email question be required?
What resource could each result point to, like a workshop, a guide or a mentor session?
guide.howToUseResponses: Group people by result and give each group a different next step: the ones ready to test might get a session on shaping a first offer, while those still exploring get a guide to customer interviews. Read the idea descriptions too, since they show what your audience is working on. Avoid presenting the result as a prediction of success.
customizeSteps: Edit the three results so each points to a resource you offer, such as a workshop, mentor or guide.
Adjust the questions and points to reflect the habits your programme values, then check the score bands still split people sensibly.
Share the link with applicants or learners, or embed it on your programme page, and export responses to plan sessions.

faqs.q: Can an entrepreneur quiz tell me if my business will succeed?
faqs.a: No. It can show which practical steps you have covered and which to do next, but many things decide whether a business works that a short quiz cannot measure.

faqs.q: What questions should an entrepreneur quiz ask?
faqs.a: Questions about what someone has done, not how they feel: customer conversations, how they would test demand, the time and money they can commit, and how they handle setbacks.

faqs.q: How are the results worked out?
faqs.a: Each answer carries points, and the total picks one of three next steps. You can change the points, bands and result text in the builder.

faqs.q: Can I use this quiz for an incubator or course intake?
faqs.a: Yes. The idea description and stage questions give you useful context, and the result helps you place people in the right session.

blocks.title: Got a business idea? A few questions about where it stands, and a practical next step at the end.
Describe your idea in a sentence or two.
Where is the idea right now?
How many people who have the problem you solve have you talked to?

options.label: A handful who actually have the problem
Ten or more who actually have the problem

blocks.title: Could you explain the problem you solve in one sentence, and have people nod?

options.label: Roughly, but it changes each time
Yes, and people recognise it straight away

blocks.title: What's the first thing you'd do to see if people want it?

options.label: Offer a simple version or pre-order and see who commits
Build the full product, then launch
Ask around and see what people think

blocks.title: How much time can you give it each week?
If it earned nothing for six months, could you keep going?

options.label: No, I'd need income from it quickly

blocks.title: Your first attempt gets a lukewarm response. What do you do?

options.label: Ask the people who said no why, and change one thing
Push on with the plan as it is
Take a break and rethink the whole thing

blocks.title: Who could you ask for help along the way? Pick all that apply.

options.label: Someone who has started a business
A local business group or course

blocks.title: Want a copy of your next step? Leave your email.

endings.title: Still exploring
endings.bodyMd: That's a fine place to be. Write down who has this problem and what they do about it today, then find three of them to talk to. You'll learn more in a week than from months of planning.

endings.title: Ready to run a small test 🚀
endings.bodyMd: You've done the groundwork. Your next step is a small, real test: a simple offer or pre-order in front of the people you've spoken to, so their actions tell you what their words can't.

endings.title: Talk to customers first
endings.bodyMd: The idea has promise, but it needs more evidence. Before you build anything, have ten honest conversations with people who have the problem, and ask about the last time it happened.
